# MARKET COMMENTARY

# Gasoline cargoes

European gasoline values declined in the Tuesday session as sources said flat prices were coming off to compensate for trade against a backdrop of elevated freight rates.

Benchmark non-oxy barge cracks to Ice Brent crude futures dropped by $6.12/bl to $36.98/bl in the Tuesday session, down from $43.10/bl on Monday.

Rapidly rising freight rates are the reason behind the fall in gasoline values in the Tuesday session, one Dubai-based trader said. Buyers cannot afford increased freight premiums at current flat prices, they said, which is leading to fob gasoline barrel premiums decreasing at ARA and in the Mediterranean.

Rates for clean freight for UKC-US Atlantic coast have twice hit $34.78/t this month, according to Argus. These are the highest transatlantic rates recorded since mid-May, and appear to be contributing to poor arbitrage economics for gasoline exports from northwest Europe to the New York Harbour region.

There has been no incentive to load spot gasoline volumes from northwest Europe for NYH at all this month, according to Argus arbitrage calculations, which would yield an average implied loss of $9.10/bl when accounting for the RBOB-Eurobob non-oxy spread, freight and value loss over the course of the two-week journey.

Similarly, UKC-west African clean freight rates reached $57.66/t on Friday and Monday this week — the highest since mid-May. The clean tanker market for both routes typically mirror one another as the routes facilitate gasoline exports from Europe to major foreign buyers in both the US and Nigeria.

## Naphtha

Naphtha prices in northwest Europe rose in the Tuesday session as buying interest appears strong so far this week, and discounts to crude narrowed on the day.

Naphtha cracks closed at a $1.60/bl discount to Ice December Brent crude futures prices at 16:30 BST (15:30 GMT), with discounts narrowing by $1.78/bl from the close on Monday.

Spanish integrated Repsol's Petronor affiliate has started up a new polymer-grade propane/propylene splitter at its 220,000 Bilbao refinery. The splitter was originally expected to come online in the first quarter of 2026. It should supply propylene to Repsol's own petrochemicals plants, including the new 300,000 t/yr polypropylene (PP) capacity expansion at its Sines facility. This is expected to be online later this year.

Repsol has not provided the capacity of the new splitter, but the 6,300 t/d fluid catalytic cracker (FCC) at Bilbao can produce about 120,000 t/yr of chemicals grade propylene, according to Argus estimates.

In Portugal, LPG demand was sharply higher on the year for a third month in August on the restart of Spanish Repsol's Sines steam cracker in June, but ongoing maintenance at the cracker and the polymers plant it supplies cut sales on the month and probably depressed volumes further in September. Propane demand increased by 38pc on the year to 716 t/d in August, but fell by the same rate on the year according to provisional figures from the energy and environment ministry's general directorate of energy and geology (DGEG). Butane demand increased by 39pc on the year to 334 t/d, but was down by 17pc from July.

The European naphtha east-west spread picked up this week, settling at an $85/t spread on Monday, a four-week high. Demand for European naphtha from the east of Suez market has remained relatively firm since July despite the east-west spread falling sharply from roughly $120/t levels in July. Data from vessel tracker Kpler points to approximately 270,000t of naphtha moving east each month between July and September. The bulk of the volume loaded for South Korea, at 108,000t in September, followed by 50,000t loading for Japan last month.

No naphtha cargo trades were reported to Argus on Tuesday. Vitol placed the most competitive bid in the window for a 28,000t cargo for 25-29 October delivery, at a $10/t premium to balance-of-month average spot prices, which normalised to $930.25/t. This tested prevailing assessments, and Argus assessments were moved 50¢/t above the bid, at $930.75/t, rising $10/t on the day.

## Diesel/Gasoil

European diesel prices rallied in Tuesday's session, after which President Trump said that the US will not import diesel from Russia.

"That diesel deal is not for us, that's being released into the world," Trump said on Tuesday. Trump's initial suggestion of the opposite went against a law the US Congress passed in March 2022 to ban imports of Russian crude and refined products, which could only be waived in consultation with Congress.

Trump's latest statement only reaffirmed market participants' belief that Russian diesel was much more likely to head to more normal destinations of Turkey and north Africa. Russia's export capacity should grow this quarter with domestic demand waning seasonally as the harvest season comes to an end. Some Russian supplies could head to Latin America, but high freight costs may limit flows on that route, an analyst said. Brazilian importers have received offers from Russian traders since Friday, a regional source said, which could free up some US Gulf Coast supply for Europe.

President Donald Trump on Tuesday said the US will not import diesel from Russia, seemingly qualifying his initial description of a deal lifting US sanctions on Russian exports of the fuel.

That law allowed future presidents to waive the ban but only in consultation with Congress. ## IMF upgrades outlook despite war risks

The global economy is holding up better than the IMF expected despite an oil supply shock triggered by the war in the Middle East, but that growth outlook could erode if the conflicts in Iran or Ukraine drag on or further escalate.

The IMF's latest World Economic Outlook forecasts the global economy will grow by 3.1pc in 2026, up by 0.1 percentage point from an update in July, with some of those gains driven by an economic rebound in Europe and robust trade flows from parts of Asia. Global growth is on track to increase to 3.4pc in 2027, unchanged from the last update, IMF said.

Rerouting energy commodity flows from the Mideast Gulf, releasing oil from strategic reserves and increasing oil production elsewhere has helped blunt disruptions from the closure of the strait of Hormuz. Overall, the disruptions in the strait have prompted the IMF to shave only 0.3 percentage points off anticipated global growth for 2026.

If not for the cushion provided by the flexibility of oil supply and a 20pc reduction in global oil intensity over the last decade, the IMF said the war in the Middle East could have cut global growth this year by three times that.

Higher oil prices contributed to China's economic growth slowing to 4.5pc this year, down from 5pc in 2025. The US

economy is expected to grow by 2.3pc, bolstered by technology-related investments in data centers. Saudi Arabia's economy is projected to shrink by 3.3pc this year because of disruptions from the Middle East war, the IMF said, whereas the comparatively less diversified economies of Bahran, Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar are on track for "double digit" economic contractions.

But some of the buffers that have mitigated the economic damage from war are running out, and energy markets are "highly sensitive" to any additional disruptions, such as an escalation in attacks on refineries or infrastructure.

"Without shoring up supply capacity and replenishing policy buffers, the global economy could soon test the limits of resilience," IMF's chief economist Silvana Tenreyro wrote in a blog post. "Dwindling energy inventories could allow geopolitical shocks to transit even more forcefully to energy prices."

Among the energy-related risks are below-average natural gas inventories in Europe that leave the continent vulnerable to extreme winter weather. Continued global depletion of energy supplies are also pushing inventories closer to "stress levels that could lead to nonlinear price adjustments", the IMF said. A prolonged stalemate or escalation in the wars in the Middle East or Ukraine could exacerbate pressure from inflation, which is on track to average 4.7pc this year, up from 4.1pc in 2025, the IMF said. The outlook anticipates global inflation in 2027 will decline to 4.1pc, although that is still 0.2 percentage points higher than the forecast from July.

Global investments into artificial intelligence (AI) have been an "offsetting force" to geopolitical headwinds, the IMF said, although that growth has been concentrated in a handful of countries that produce advanced microchips, such as Taiwan and South Korea, or that are building out data centers, such as China and the US. That investment boom is contributing to near-term inflationary pressures, the IMF said, and any future re-reassessment of AI-related profitability could sharply curtail investment and tighten financial conditions.

Global growth in 2027 could end up being "materially lower", and inflation "significantly higher", under a risk scenario the IMF developed under which higher commodity prices and concerns over government debt causes a reassessment of borrowing risks, Tenreyro said. Keeping publicly held debt on a "sustainable path" could prevent that scenario, she said.

Higher oil prices contributed to China's economic growth slowing to 4.5pc this year, down from 5pc in 2025. The US

economy is expected to grow by 2.3pc, bolstered by technology-related investments in data centers. Saudi Arabia's economy is projected to shrink by 3.3pc this year because of disruptions from the Middle East war, the IMF said, whereas the comparatively less diversified economies of Bahran, Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar are on track for "double digit" economic contractions.

But some of the buffers that have mitigated the economic damage from war are running out, and energy markets are "highly sensitive" to any additional disruptions, such as an escalation in attacks on refineries or infrastructure.

"Without shoring up supply capacity and replenishing policy buffers, the global economy could soon test the limits of resilience," IMF's chief economist Silvana Tenreyro wrote in a blog post. "Dwindling energy inventories could allow geopolitical shocks to transit even more forcefully to energy prices."

Among the energy-related risks are below-average natural gas inventories in Europe that leave the continent vulnerable to extreme winter weather. Continued global depletion of energy supplies are also pushing inventories closer to "stress levels that could lead to nonlinear price adjustments", the IMF said. A prolonged stalemate or escalation in the wars in the Middle East or Ukraine could exacerbate pressure from inflation, which is on track to average 4.7pc this year, up from 4.1pc in 2025, the IMF said. The outlook anticipates global inflation in 2027 will decline to 4.1pc, although that is still 0.2 percentage points higher than the forecast from July.

Global investments into artificial intelligence (AI) have been an "offsetting force" to geopolitical headwinds, the IMF said, although that growth has been concentrated in a handful of countries that produce advanced microchips, such as Taiwan and South Korea, or that are building out data centers, such as China and the US. That investment boom is contributing to near-term inflationary pressures, the IMF said, and any future re-reassessment of AI-related profitability could sharply curtail investment and tighten financial conditions.

Global growth in 2027 could end up being "materially lower", and inflation "significantly higher", under a risk scenario the IMF developed under which higher commodity prices and concerns over government debt causes a reassessment of borrowing risks, Tenreyro said. Keeping publicly held debt on a "sustainable path" could prevent that scenario, she said.

### Change to Eurobob gasoline assessments: Update

Argus has observed that bids, offers and trade in the Eurobob gasoline market remain discussed as a differential to the underlying Eurobob oxy gasoline swap and have not transitioned to refer to the increasingly liquid trade in Eurobob non-oxy gasoline swaps. As a result, Argus will assess Eurobob oxy and non-oxy barge markets based on their differentials to whatever floating price reference is commonly used by the market, rather than solely against the Eurobob non-oxy swap price as previously stated.

Should Eurobob oxy and non-oxy barges trade at differentials to different underlying derivatives prices, Argus will standardise that market information to a common differential basis. The common differential basis will be the one used for the larger share of physical Eurobob non-oxy barge trades on the day of assessment.

Argus will revisit this aspect of the Eurobob methodology should market conditions change.

Following industry consultation and effective 1 January 2024, Argus will assess the Eurobob oxy gasoline barge price as a differential to the Eurobob non-oxy barge price. There has been strong support from market participants for the change because E10 is now the primary grade in the northwest European gasoline market.

In addition, from 1 January 2024, Argus will use bids, offers and trades for Eurobob oxy and Eurobob non-oxy barges that are expressed as a differential to the Eurobob non-oxy futures price to assess the price of both gasoline grades.

### Continuation of Argus Eurobob oxy assessment

Following requests from market participants, Argus confirms previous guidance that it will continue to publish the Eurobob oxy barge assessment and that it has no plans to discontinue the assessment. Argus notes strong interest from market participants to continue to actively trade both Eurobob oxy and Eurobob non-oxy barges.

### New Eurobob oxy methodology from 1 January 2024

From 1 January 2024, the Eurobob oxy price will be constructed as follows:

- Volume weighted averages of the differentials at which Eurobob oxy and Eurobob non-oxy barges have traded against the common floating Eurobob derivative price will be calculated;
- Then the difference between those volume-weighted averages will be subtracted from the final Eurobob non-oxy price assessment for that day to arrive at the Eurobob oxy barge price assessment;
- The common differential basis will be the one used for the larger share of physical Eurobob non-oxy barge trades on the day of assessment.

### Eurobob non-oxy derivatives are already available for trade

A full range of financial derivatives referencing Argus Eurobob non-oxy gasoline barge assessments are already listed on futures exchanges, and these assessments have been part of Argus' annual assurance review under the IOSCO principles since 2019.

### Eurobob oxy prices to continue beyond the end of 2024

- Argus will continue to publish the Eurobob oxy barge price beyond 31 December 2024, assessed as a differential to the Eurobob non-oxy barge price as described above.
- A legacy volume-weighted-average price for Eurobob oxy barges, calculated as the volume-weighted average of the outright $/t prices of Eurobob oxy barge trades, will be published after 1 January 2024, but with a new Argus code.

### Clarification of European Russian-origin product restrictions

For the avoidance of doubt, beginning with prices assessed on 22 December, for all European product prices, except those under the header "Russian refined products", Argus will align its definition of Russian origin with that of EU (and/or UK, where applicable) sanctions regulation. On 22 December, Argus will simplify its previous definitions of non-Russian origin in the Argus European Products methodology, which will be replaced with "compliant with all EU sanctions in force or scheduled to be in force on 21 January 2026, including but not limited to Article 3ma of council regulation 833/2014".

Issue 26-198 | Tuesday 13 October 2026

### Argus successfully completes annual losco assurance review

Argus has completed the 13th external assurance review of its price benchmarks covering crude oil, oil products, LPG, chemicals, thermal and coking coal, natural gas, biofuels, biomass, metals, fertilizers and agricultural markets. The review was carried out by professional services firm PwC. Annual independent, external reviews of oil benchmarks are required by international regulatory group losco's Principles for Oil Price Reporting Agencies, and losco encourages extension of the reviews to non-oil benchmarks. For more information and to download the review visit our website www.argusmedia.com/en/about-us/governance-compliance

### Eurobob gasoline seasonal transition dates

Argus Eurobob gasoline barge price assessments will be based only on information about trade in winter grades until 23 March 2026, and based only on summer grades from 27 March 2026 until 22 September 2026. The assessments will be based only on winter grades from 28 September 2026.

During the 24-26 March and 23-25 September seasonal transition periods, at least 3,000t of summer-specification trade and 3,000t of winter-specification trade are required to calculate the volume-weighted average. If less than 3,000t of trade of either grade within Argus' criteria is reported, Argus will include in the volume-weighted average an assessment of the prevailing market price for the relevant grade at 4:30pm London time. That assessment will be assigned whatever volume is required such that the total volume of reported trades and the assessment for that grade equals 3,000t.

### Subscriber notice: Gasoline barges

For trades to be included in Argus gasoline barge assessments, standard nomination procedures must be followed. The buyer should give two working days' notice of barge ETA. Nominations received after 14:00 London time or on Fridays after 13:00 London time will be deemed to be received on the following working day. Otherwise, the original day of nomination will count as day one of the two days notice.

Quality testing: On gasoline barges, standard industry practice assumes seller's discretion to appoint an inspections company from a list of widely recognised entities. But if a buyer has reasonable cause* to request an alternative but widely recognised inspector, the nominated inspection company should be changed by mutual agreement. If changing the nominated inspection company is not acceptable to the seller, the seller should agree to allow a re-test of the product by an alternative inspections company before loading.

*Reasonable cause may include recent history of deviations between test results at loadport and/or on delivery, where the deviation is in excess of industry accepted margins of reproducibility and repeatability.

### Using EU ETS-inclusive WS tanker rates

Following consultation, Argus tanker rates will use the version of flat rates published by the Worldscale Association that include EU emissions trading system (ETS) costs.

Argus Tanker Freight will continue to publish a selection of ETS costs for tankers as Carbon Costs of Freight (CCFs).

To discuss this announcement, please contact freightteam@argusmedia.com
